Now, with the full context for both the objective function (Figure 10, growth rate) and constraint (Figure 11, TCS contamination in the necking region) we can begin to start identifying an optimal reactor design and associated operating conditions. In contrast to Figure 10, perhaps the most evident trend in the TCS sensitivity is that narrower chamber heights are associated with more incursion of TCS into the neck area and an increased likelihood of fouling, or undesirable deposition outside the reaction chamber. This trade-off between designs that aggressively maximize growth rate at the expense of limiting TCS invasion, or minimize TCS invasion while stifling growth rate, is at the heart of this design problem. To better understand these competing factors and their relative sensitivities to the variables we have thus far found to exert the largest and clearest effects, we more formally calculate the sensitivity of both the objective and constraint values with respect to each of our independent controls and present the analysis in Figures 12 and 13. Figure 12: The average growth rate’s sensitivity with respect to each of the 8 control variables computed in two different ways, S1 refers to the first-order Sobol indices and delta is the delta index from Plischke et al. [7], these values differ in the exact metrics and calculations used to assign importance but the interpretation of both is that higher bars indicate that the growth rate is more sensitive to that parameter. Figure 13: The median molar fraction of TCS’s sensitivity to our 8 control variables, as in Figure 12, higher bars indicate that the molar fraction of TCS is more sensitive to changes in that quantity. Figure 12 offers further understanding of how much more important one variable is on the overall outcome versus another. For example, our intuition that chamber height plays a role in the growth rate is confirmed, as both sensitivity indices report this being the control variable that has the largest effect on growth rate. Both sensitivity indices also agree that the second most important control variable is the reactor operating pressure. Figure 13 further underlines the importance of the chamber height on the molar fraction of TCS. From our scatter plots, we understand that these two model outputs, molar fraction of TCS and growth rate, tend to move us toward different reactor designs with respect to chamber height, i.e., minimizing TCS contamination is accomplished with large chamber heights and maximizing growth rate is accomplished with small chamber heights.
